result.reason: The passage presents Rami bar Ḥama's argument that this is a biblical oath based on Deuteronomy 19:15 and the ed echad principle, which is precisely what the 'Rami Bar Chama Position' prose section describes — the current placement under 'Shnayim/Echad Rule' is too late in the logical sequence, as that section's prose covers the crystallized general principle as a conclusion to Rami's reasoning, whereas this passage is the argument itself.

The passage contains Rava's full statement with BOTH objections, and candidate 0 ('Oath Taker Benefits') is the heading that introduces Rava's response and his first objection — the natural home for the complete quoted text that encompasses both answers together, rather than splitting it under the second objection's heading.
The passage is Rava's direct statement that the oath is rabbinic and instituted to appease the husband, which is precisely what the 'D'Rabbanan to Appease' section's prose describes and analyzes.
Both items together constitute Rav Pappa's statement about the clever husband's strategy, which is precisely what heading 1 ('Husband's Clever Move') introduces in its prose.

Both items are part of the continuous dispute-and-resolution chain about the 'two ketubot' defense: item 1 (Rav Sheisha's fix) leads into item 2 (Rav Ashi's objection that she can claim two ketubot and his resolution), which is precisely what the 'Two Ketubos Defense' prose section describes.

The passage quotes the mishnah from Shvuot about orphans/heirs collecting only by oath, which is precisely what the 'Shvuot Mishnah' section's prose describes as the Gemara adducing a parallel from that mishnah.

Item 1 is precisely the Gemara's question about why heirs must swear when their father could collect without an oath — matching heading 0's prose exactly — and Item 2 is Rav Zerika/Rav Yehuda's qualification that follows directly from that resolution, both belonging together under 'Why Heirs Swear' rather than the current 'Complete Denial Rule' heading.

Both items present Rava's objection and Rav Zerika's corrected ruling that when heirs claim their father never borrowed (lo lovisi), the creditor collects without an oath — precisely what the 'Heirs Say Father Paid' prose describes as the inverted ruling distinguishing the paid vs. never-borrowed scenarios.

The passage directly contains Rav Acha Sar HaBira's ruling about 'lo shanu ela kesubas isha mishum china' and the distinction between a wife's ketubah and an ordinary creditor, which is precisely what the 'Mishum China Rationale' section's prose describes.

The passage quotes Rava citing Rav Nachman extending collection rights to an ordinary creditor (baal chov), which is precisely what heading 3 'Rava's Broad Rule' describes — the current placement under 'Creditor Protection' is too late in the sequence.

All four items together cover exactly the content described in heading 4 ('Maintenance & Ketubah'): Rabbi Shimon's distinction between mezonot and ketubah claims, the lo shanya formulation, and Rav Sheshet's objection about the word 'heirs' — all of which the prose of heading 4 explicitly discusses.

The passage is Rav Sheshet's proposal of a different context (the apotropos scenario) to explain Rabbi Shimon's use of 'heirs,' which matches the 'Apotropos Context' heading's prose about Rav Sheshes proposing this different context.

The passage introduces the Abba Shaul/Rabbis dispute by quoting the mishna from Gittin, which is precisely what the 'Abba Shaul Debate' section prose describes — the existence of a separate Tannaitic dispute about when an apotropos must swear — rather than belonging under 'Abba Shaul Position' which discusses only Abba Shaul's specific ruling.

Both items — Rav Sheshet's alignment of Rabbi Shimon with Abba Shaul and Abaye's grammatical objection about 'kol zman' vs. 'im' — are precisely the content described in the 'Shimon = Abba Shaul' prose, which explicitly covers this reading and Abaye's challenge to it.

Both items together constitute Abaye's explanation that Rabbi Shimon's ruling connects to the dispute between Abba Shaul and the Rabbis — precisely the content described in candidate 2's prose about Abba Shaul's position that the husband cannot waive the orphans' protection oath.

The passage is Rav Pappa's objection asking what the second clause (when she does not demand her ketubah) adds, which directly matches the prose of candidate 1 describing Rav Papa's question about the second half of Rabbi Shimon's formulation.

The passage explains Rav Pappa's clarification that Rabbi Shimon's position excludes both Rabbi Eliezer and the Chachamim, establishing that heirs can only administer oaths when she collects her ketubah — which is precisely what the 'Shimon Balanced' section's prose describes.
